stops.name: Jargeau, the storming of the town
stops.campa: The Loire campaign opens against Suffolk in Jargeau. When the captains hesitate at the English numbers, she tells them not to fear any multitude: God guides the work, and were she not sure of it she would rather keep sheep. In the assault she plucks the young Duke of Alençon from the spot where a stone-gun is trained, and the gentleman who takes his place there dies. On the ladder a stone bursts on her helmet; she rises crying that the English are ours. Jargeau is carried; Suffolk yields himself, they say, to the most valiant woman in the world.
stops.quote: Move from this place, or that engine will kill you.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Jean, Duke of Alençon, rehabilitation trial (1456)

stops.name: Meung-sur-Loire, the bridge taken
stops.campa: Without pausing to savor Jargeau, the army swings downriver. In one sharp evening action the French seize the fortified bridge of Meung out of the hands of its English guard, set their own garrison on it, and cut the river road between Talbot's garrisons. The Maid is in the press of it as always, her standard the moving heart of the army; the men now believe that where the standard goes the matter is already decided in heaven, and follow it as they would follow fire. Meung's castle still holds for England behind them; it does not matter. The campaign has become a single week-long motion.

stops.name: Beaugency, the surrender and the Constable's welcome
stops.campa: The English garrison, cannon-battered and cut off, yields the castle of Beaugency by composition and marches out with their lives. Into the camp, uninvited and half in disgrace, rides Arthur de Richemont, Constable of France, with his Bretons; the king's favorite would send him away, and Alençon threatens to leave. Jehanne rides to meet him. The Constable says he does not know if she is of God, but if she is he does not fear her. She judges the hour. Fastolf and Talbot are near with a fresh army. She takes his alliance, and the army turns as one to meet the English in the open.
stops.quote: Ah, fair Constable, you are not come by my will; but since you are come, you are welcome.
stops.quote_source: Guillaume Gruel, Chronique d'Arthur de Richemont

stops.name: Patay, the English broken in the field
stops.campa: The captains ask what to do, for the English have turned at bay in open country: the thing France has dreaded since Agincourt. She answers that though they hung from the clouds we shall have them. A stag bursting from cover betrays the English position; La Hire's vanguard strikes before the archers can plant their stakes, and the army of Fastolf and Talbot is destroyed on the road by Patay: thousands fallen, Talbot taken, Fastolf in flight. Agincourt is answered in an afternoon. She grieves that evening over a dying prisoner, holding his head while he is confessed.
stops.quote: In God's name, though they hung from the clouds we shall have them, for God has sent us to punish them. Today the gentle King shall have the greatest victory he has ever had; my counsel has told me they are all ours.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Jean, Duke of Alençon, rehabilitation trial (1456)

stops.name: Gien, the army of the anointing gathers
stops.campa: To Gien comes the king, and to Gien she summons France. Against the counselors who call the road to Reims impossible, citing Burgundian towns, no siege train, she sets the single argument of her voices: the Dauphin must be anointed at Reims, and the towns will open. Twelve thousand men gather without pay, gentlemen coming as archers for the love of the thing. From Gien her letters fly out to the good towns; to loyal Tournai, islanded in enemy land, she writes the week's news: in eight days the English have been chased from all the Loire, and the king goes now to his sacring.
stops.quote: Loyal Frenchmen of the town of Tournai, the Maid sends you news: in eight days she has chased the English out of all the places they held on the river Loire... Come to the anointing of the gentle King Charles at Reims, where we shall shortly be.
stops.quote_source: Letter to the citizens of Tournai, 25 June 1429

stops.name: Auxerre, the closed city passed by
stops.campa: The first Burgundian city on the road neither opens nor fights. Auxerre treats: provisions sold to the army at the gates, a promise of such obedience as Troyes and Châlons shall render, and, the whisper runs, a quiet purse for La Trémoille. The Maid would test the walls; the council will not. She, who four months before knelt unknown in the cathedral within, now watches its towers from the camp of a royal army. The lesson of the coronation road is set here: the towns will come to the king one by one, like the tide taking back a shore, and the sword will mostly stay sheathed.

stops.name: Troyes: the city of the shameful treaty opens its gates
stops.campa: Troyes, where the treaty was signed that gave France to England, shuts its gates; the army starves before it on boiled wheat and the counselors talk of turning back. The old councillor Robert le Maçon asks the Maid's word: in two days, she says, the city is the king's, by love or by force. All night she orders the siege like a veteran, throwing fascines into the ditches, siting the guns; at first light, when she cries the assault, the city yields. Brother Richard comes out sprinkling holy water against the demon he fears she is; she tells him to approach boldly; she will not fly away.
stops.quote: Approach boldly — I shall not fly away.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 3 March 1431 (her own account of Brother Richard)

stops.name: Châlons, the men of Domrémy on the road
stops.campa: Châlons opens without a blow, its bishop bearing the keys, and the road to Reims lies clear. Here, in the middle of the king's triumph, four or five men of Domrémy stand waiting in the crowd: neighbors who have walked across a war to see Jacques d'Arc's daughter beside the King of France. She greets Gérardin d'Épinal, the one Burgundian sympathizer of her village, whose child she held at the font, and gives a coat she has worn to another. To Gérardin she says the one dark sentence of the coronation road, and it will keep: she fears nothing but treachery.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Gérardin d'Épinal of Domrémy, rehabilitation trial (1456)

stops.name: Reims, the coronation of Charles VII
stops.campa: Reims opens on the eve; all night the town makes ready. On Sunday, in the cathedral of the kings, four knights on horseback escort the Sainte Ampoule into the nave, and Charles is anointed with the oil of Clovis and crowned true King of France. Throughout the rite Jehanne stands beside the altar in armor, her standard in her hand: it had borne the burden; it was right it should have the honor. At the end she kneels weeping at the king's feet, and all who see her weep also. In the crowd stands her father, lodged at the inn of the Striped Ass; the city pays his bill.
stops.quote: Gentle King, now is accomplished the pleasure of God, who willed that I should raise the siege of Orléans and bring you to this city of Reims to receive your holy anointing, showing that you are true king, and he to whom the kingdom of France must belong.

stops.name: Crépy-en-Valois, 'here is a good people'
stops.campa: The anointed king rides down through lands that turn French at his coming, Soissons, Château-Thierry, Provins, while Bedford maneuvers and writes insolent letters. Riding between La Ferté and Crépy-en-Valois through crowds crying Noël, between the archbishop of Reims and the Bastard, Jehanne speaks of her own end for the first time in the canon: would that she might be buried in this good soil when she dies. Asked where she expects to die, she answers: where it pleases God; she knows neither the hour nor the place; would that God let her go home now to her brothers and sisters, who would be so glad to see her.
stops.quote: Here is a good people! Never have I seen a people so rejoice at the coming of so noble a king. Would that I might be so happy, when my days end, as to be buried in this soil.

stops.name: Saint-Denis, the cry of France
stops.campa: With Alençon and the vanguard she seizes the abbey-town of Saint-Denis, necropolis of the kings, whose very name is the war-cry of the realm. From here for a fortnight she and the duke ride daily to the gates of Paris, skirmishing from the Porte Saint-Honoré to Montmartre, sounding the walls of the greatest city of the West. Twice Alençon rides back to draw the reluctant king forward from his negotiations; Burgundy has beguiled the council with truces that spend the summer. She waits under the abbey towers among the tombs of the kings, sharpening the army for the assault she believes her Lord has left in her hands.

stops.name: Paris, the assault on the Porte Saint-Honoré
stops.campa: On the feast of Our Lady's Nativity the assault goes in against the Porte Saint-Honoré. Jehanne carries her standard down into the first ditch, crosses the swine-market ridge, and stands at the lip of the great water-ditch sounding the depth with her lance-shaft, crying to Paris to yield to the King of France. A crossbow bolt pierces her thigh; her standard-bearer is shot through the head. Wounded, she will not go back, urging the assault from the ditch-edge into full night, until the captains carry her away against her will. Tomorrow, she says, they would have taken it. The king orders retreat instead.
stops.quote: It is good and right to keep the festival of the Blessed Mary; and in my conscience I hold it good to keep the feast of Our Lady from the beginning to the end.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 3 March 1431 (asked whether it was well done to assault Paris on the feast)
